--- title: "How much data a network needs" description: "A network needs enough rows for the signal to stand out from the noise, not a fixed number. Learning curves compare a network with linear regression and a random forest as the survey grows, and the expected counts check what the network learned." order: 4 categories: [neural-networks, generalisation] --- ## Learning curves show how error falls with more data "Neural networks need a lot of data" is common advice, but it does not say how much, and marine surveys usually have hundreds of rows, not millions. This page measures it on a survey of that size. The answer depends on how noisy the response is as much as on the number of rows, and that tells you when a network is worth trying on your own data. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: A **learning curve** plots a model's error on new data against the number of rows it was trained on. The error falls as rows are added and levels off above the **noise**, the part of each value that no model can predict; [The bias–variance trade-off](../05-generalisation/bias-variance.qmd) showed that on this survey the noise is the largest part of the error. A flexible model such as a network usually starts behind a simple one, because with few rows its many weights fit the noise. With more rows it can overtake, and the noisier the response, the more rows that takes. ::: {.diagram} ![Learning curves: error on new data falls as training rows are added and levels off above the noise. A flexible model starts behind a simple one and overtakes it once there are enough rows; the noisier the data, the more rows that takes.](img/learning-curves.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Learning curve, error against rows: a curve of error on new data falls steeply, then levels off above a dashed line marked noise. Two models, simple and flexible: the simple model's curve falls fast and levels off; the flexible model's curve starts higher, falls further and crosses below it at a marked point. Noise, signal against noise: two small panels with the same two curves and a dashed line marked your survey. With low noise the curves cross after few rows, well before the line; with high noise they cross only after it. A note says to judge rows relative to noise."} ::: ## Worked example Three models predict abundance from eight inputs: depth, temperature, chlorophyll, salinity, substrate, season, longitude and latitude. They are linear regression, the random forest from [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) and the network that `mlp()` fitted on [Training a network](training-a-network.qmd), with eight hidden units and a small penalty. A quarter of the sites are held back as test sites, split by site as on [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |> select(station_id, site_id, abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season, longitude, latitude) |> drop_na() set.seed(99) split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season + longitude + latitude base_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_zv(all_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) baseline <- rmse_vec(test$abundance, rep(mean(train$abundance), nrow(test))) c(training = nrow(train), test = nrow(test)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> training test #> 539 181 ``` ::: ::: `step_zv()` drops any column with the same value in every row, which a 0/1 column for a rare substrate can be in a small sample. Predicting the mean count of the training stations at every test station gives an RMSE of 4.72 individuals: a model has to beat that to have learned anything. ### The forest leads at every survey size Training sets of 40, 80, 160 and 320 stations are drawn from the 539 training stations, ten draws at each size, and each model is scored on the same test stations. The ten fits with all the stations differ only in their random seed, which for the network sets its starting weights. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} models <- list( `Linear regression` = linear_reg(), `Random forest` = rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("regression"), `Neural network` = mlp(hidden_units = 8, penalty = 0.01, epochs = 500) |> set_engine("nnet") |> set_mode("regression") ) sizes <- c(40, 80, 160, 320, nrow(train)) learning_curve <- function(recipe, target) { map_dfr(1:10, \(draw) map_dfr(sizes, \(n) { set.seed(1000 * draw + n) rows <- train[sample(nrow(train), n), ] map_dfr(names(models), \(model) { set.seed(draw) fitted <- fit(workflow(recipe, models[[model]]), rows) tibble(draw, n, model, rmse = rmse_vec(test[[target]], predict(fitted, test)$.pred)) }) })) } curves <- learning_curve(base_recipe, "abundance") curves |> summarise(rmse = round(mean(rmse), 2), .by = c(n, model)) |> pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rmse) |> rename(`Training stations` = n) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Training stations| Linear regression| Random forest| Neural network| |-----------------:|-----------------:|-------------:|--------------:| | 40| 5.17| 4.61| 5.56| | 80| 4.69| 4.47| 6.77| | 160| 4.49| 4.36| 7.27| | 320| 4.37| 4.32| 5.48| | 539| 4.32| 4.20| 4.94|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} curves |> summarise(lower = min(rmse), upper = max(rmse), rmse = mean(rmse), .by = c(n, model)) |> ggplot(aes(n, rmse, colour = model, fill = model)) + geom_hline(yintercept = baseline, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.8) + annotate("text", x = 90, y = baseline, label = "Predict the mean", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.6, size = 3.4, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + scale_x_log10(breaks = sizes) + labs(x = "Training stations (log scale)", y = "RMSE on test sites (individuals)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Test RMSE against the number of training stations, ten draws at each size; at the largest size the draws use all the training stations and differ only in their seed. Ribbons span the lowest to highest of the ten draws. The dashed line is the score for predicting the mean.](how-much-data_files/figure-html/fig-learning-curves-1.png){#fig-learning-curves fig-alt='Three lines with shaded ribbons, test RMSE against training stations on a log scale from 40 to 539. A dashed line at 4.72 marks predicting the mean. The random forest is lowest at every size, from 4.61 at 40 stations to 4.20 with all of them. Linear regression starts at 5.17, above the dashed line, falls quickly and ends at 4.32. The neural network is highest, with the widest ribbon; it rises to 7.27 at 160 stations, then falls steeply to 4.94.' width=1560} ::: ::: With 40 stations, linear regression scores 5.17 and the network 5.56, both worse than predicting the mean; only the forest beats it. Small samples are hard on every model that estimates many numbers, not only on networks. Linear regression improves quickly and levels off at 4.32. The forest, which averages 500 trees, leads at every size and ends at 4.20. The network has 113 weights, and its curve shows what that costs on a few hundred noisy counts. Its scores vary most between draws of the same size, by a standard deviation of 1.52 at 80 stations, so a single fit of it can be far from typical. After 160 stations it improves the fastest of the three, from 7.27 to 4.94 with all 539, and its curve is still falling steeply where the data run out. ### Cross-validation shrinks the network to one unit The eight-unit network was not tuned. Cross-validation by site, as on [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd), chooses the number of hidden units and the penalty from the training stations. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tunable <- mlp(hidden_units = tune(), penalty = tune(), epochs = 500) |> set_engine("nnet") |> set_mode("regression") set.seed(11) folds <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = site_id, v = 5) set.seed(12) searched <- tune_grid( workflow(base_recipe, tunable), resamples = folds, grid = expand_grid(hidden_units = c(1, 2, 4, 8), penalty = c(0.01, 0.1, 1)), metrics = metric_set(rmse) ) show_best(searched, metric = "rmse", n = 4) |> transmute(`Hidden units` = hidden_units, Penalty = penalty, `Mean RMSE` = round(mean, 2), `Standard error` = round(std_err, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Hidden units| Penalty| Mean RMSE| Standard error| |------------:|-------:|---------:|--------------:| | 1| 1.0| 4.32| 0.33| | 2| 1.0| 4.57| 0.29| | 2| 0.1| 4.61| 0.39| | 4| 1.0| 4.61| 0.33|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} best <- select_best(searched, metric = "rmse") set.seed(7) tuned <- workflow(base_recipe, tunable) |> finalize_workflow(best) |> fit(train) tuned_rmse <- rmse_vec(test$abundance, predict(tuned, test)$.pred) tibble(`Test RMSE` = round(tuned_rmse, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Test RMSE| |---------:| | 4.42|
::: ::: The search chooses **one hidden unit with a penalty of 1**, the smallest network on the grid with the largest penalty. That is cross-validation doing its job: with this much noise, the extra flexibility costs more in variance than it gains, so the search picks the network closest to a straight line. On the test sites it scores 4.42, against 4.94 for the untuned network and 4.32 for linear regression. ### The expected counts show what the network learned A real survey stops there. This one is simulated, so each station's **expected count**, the average the simulation drew its count from, is known, as on [The bias–variance trade-off](../05-generalisation/bias-variance.qmd). Refitting the three models with the expected count as the target, and scoring them against the expected counts at the test sites, removes the noise and shows how well each model learned the response itself. It is a check only: no real dataset has this column. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_data <- load_coastal_survey_truth() train <- left_join(train, check_data, by = "station_id") test <- left_join(test, check_data, by = "station_id") expected_recipe <- recipe(update(predictors, true_mean ~ .), data = train) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_zv(all_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) checked <- learning_curve(expected_recipe, "true_mean") checked |> summarise(rmse = round(mean(rmse), 2), .by = c(n, model)) |> pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rmse) |> rename(`Training stations` = n) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Training stations| Linear regression| Random forest| Neural network| |-----------------:|-----------------:|-------------:|--------------:| | 40| 2.75| 2.30| 2.50| | 80| 2.34| 2.10| 2.50| | 160| 2.20| 1.89| 1.85| | 320| 2.15| 1.74| 1.51| | 539| 2.12| 1.63| 1.54|
::: ::: The order turns round. From 160 stations on, the network is the closest of the three to the expected counts: this is the crossing in the diagram above. With all 539 stations it scores 1.54, against 1.63 for the forest and 2.12 for linear regression, 27% better than linear regression. Linear regression levels off because a straight line cannot follow the humped responses in the survey; the network can, and from a few hundred stations it did. So the network was **short of signal, not of rows**. It learned the response well; on the observed counts the noise around each expected count hid that gain. ## Judge a survey's size against its noise The number of rows alone does not say whether a network will pay off. What matters is how much of the response is signal. You cannot compute expected counts for real data, but you can estimate the noise: from duplicate tows, replicate grabs, or two observers counting the same sample. A response measured with little noise, such as a well-calibrated sensor reading, leaves much more signal per row than a count, and there a network reaches its advantage with far fewer stations. Two signs in your own learning curves help. If the network's curve is still falling with all the data, more stations would help it. If cross-validation picks the smallest network on the grid, a simpler model will do as well for now. [When a network is the right tool](when-to-use-one.qmd) shows a problem where a network wins with a few hundred rows. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it Each observed count is its expected count plus noise, $y = \mu(x) + \varepsilon$. On new data the expected squared error of a model $\hat f$ is $E[(y - \hat f(x))^2] = \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} + \sigma^2$, where $\sigma^2$ is the variance of the noise. More rows shrink the variance, and a flexible model has the smaller bias, but $\sigma^2$ stays. When $\sigma^2$ is large, the flexible model's lower bias is a small share of the error, and its larger variance can cost more than it gains. Scoring against $\mu(x)$ instead of $y$ removes $\sigma^2$ and shows the bias and variance alone. ::: ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A **learning curve** plots error on new data against the number of training rows. It shows whether more data would help and where one model overtakes another. - With 539 training stations, the random forest led at every size and the eight-unit network varied most between draws. - **Cross-validation shrank the network** to one hidden unit with the largest penalty, close to linear regression, because the counts are noisy. - Scored against the expected counts, the network learned the response best, 27% better than linear regression. It was **short of signal, not of rows**. - Judge a survey's size against its noise: the less noisy the response, the fewer rows a network needs. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Replace `abundance` with the presence column `present` and RMSE with `roc_auc`, using `set_mode("classification")`. Presence is less noisy than the count: does the network catch up with the forest sooner? 2. Add `mlp(hidden_units = 8, penalty = 1)` to `models`. How much of the eight-unit network's spread between draws does the larger penalty remove?
